newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM signals cabinet of veteran politicians.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM signals cabinet of veteran politicians.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto retained key policymakers in their party posts on Tuesday in a sign that his new cabinet is likely to feature mainly veteran politicians.

Hashimoto, forced to form a minority government after failing to put together a new coalition, is to be formally re-elected prime minister in a short special session of parliament on Thursday and is expected to announce his cabinet shortly after.

A party spokesman said Hashimoto had decided that the two top executives of his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) -- secretary-general Koichi Kato and policy affairs chief Taku Yamasaki -- would keep their jobs.

Kato's reappointment was seen as critical to maintaining the LDP's fragile alliance with the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake party after the two parties shied away from again joining an LDP-led coalition, analysts said.

The conservative LDP fell 12 seats short of a majority in a general election last month and sought in vain for coalition partners in a bid to command comfortable majorities in both houses of parliament. Sakigake and the Social Democrats had cabinet members in the outgoing government.

Kato and Yamasaki played key roles in helping the LDP cobble together a loose "out-of-cabinet" alliance with its two old partners, who fared badly in the election and blamed their poor showing on too formal ties with the LDP.
After finalising the party leadership on Tuesday, Hashimoto started back-room manoeuvring to pick his cabinet colleagues.

Outgoing Health Minister Naoto Kan, once a member of Sakigake and now co-leader of the opposition Democratic Party, said Hashimoto looked likely to return to an old-style cabinet decided by factions within the LDP.
"It is factional politics as usual," he told reporters.
Among names floated for key cabinet posts were former LDP executive Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, head of the LDP's second biggest faction and a former trade, transport and foreign minister.

Domestic media said Mitsuzuka was a possible contender for powerful economic portfolios, including finance minister, as was Shizuka Kamei, an outspoken former transport minister who currently heads the LDP's press office.
"Mitsuzuka has got power, he is experienced, and he knows policy," a senior LDP official said.
Analysts saw a certain irony in talk that Kamei might win the finance post, given his opposition earlier to a rise in the sales tax to five percent from three percent next April.

The tax increase has been approved, but the LDP, the Social Democrats and Sakigake agreed last week to review it and the whole tax system as part of a policy pact that forms the basis for their loose cooperation.
"Putting the biggest opponent (of a policy) in a position where he can no longer oppose it is a time-honoured tactic," one political analyst said.

Whoever becomes finance minister faces a tough agenda, including implementing the sales tax increase, determining the need for a stimulative extra budget for the current fiscal year, and crafting the 1997/98 budget.
Another headache will be how to deal with proposals to trim the power of the Finance Ministry, which is under fire for its handling of banking woes and scandals involving its officials.

Analysts said the floating of old-guard names such as Mitsuzuka and Kamei for key posts could well give the impression that Hashimoto is not serious about the reforms many say are vital to ensure Japan's global competitiveness.
